# Overview

Healthcare associated infections (HAIs) are a major problem in United States hospital systems. HAIs is linked to many factors, such as the patient's age or stay at a hospital, as well as the the hospital's infrastructure (e.g. number of available beds at the hospital) and staffing. Knowing how these factors affect patients is key for hospital leaders and institutions to implement policies in slowing down HCIs and better patient care. 

The main research question of this analysis is how do both patient and hospital factors contribute to a patient's infection risk?

# Data Description and Processing

The dataset contains data collected from hospitals in the United States, with each row representing one hospital.

We categorized the variables in the data set in terms of "patient factors" and "hospital factors":

Patient factors:
Stay (numeric): average length of patient stay (days)

Age (numeric): average patient age (years)

Culture (numeric): Ratio of number of cultures performed to number of patients without signs or
symptoms of hospital-acquired infection, times 100.

Xray (numeric): Ratio of number of X-rays performed to number of patients without signs or symptoms of pneumonia, times 100.

Hospital factors:
Beds (numeric): Average number of beds in hospital during study period.

MedSchool (factor): Hospital has an associated medical school: 1 =Yes, 2=No --> We decided to factor this variable as there are different "groups" or levels for medical school (1 or 2). 

Region (factor): Geographic region, where: 1 =NE, 2=NC, 3=S, 4=W --> We decided to factor this variable as there are different "groups" of regions. 

Census (numeric): Average number of patients in hospital per day during study period.

Nurses (numeric): Average number of full-time equivalent registered and licensed practical nurses during study period (number full-time plus one half the number part time).

Facilities (numeric): Percent of 35 potential facilities and services that are provided by the hospital.

Outcome: 
InfctRsk (numeric): Average estimated probability of acquiring infection in hospital (percent)

The data set was checked for missing values. Of the original 116 observations, we removed 3 observations that contained missing values leaving 113 complete observations.

We used the InfctRsk (infection risk) variable as our outcome. 

```{R}
# Read the dataset and set it to a dataframe 
infection.df = read.csv("dataset2.csv")

infection.df = na.omit(infection.df)

infection.df$MedSchool = factor(infection.df$MedSchool)
infection.df$Region = factor(infection.df$Region)
```
# Data Exploration

In figure 1, the distribution of the outcome variable, infection risk (named in our dataset as InfctRsk), shows an approximately normal distribution, with only one peak. The density curve fits the data pretty well. 


```{R}
hist(infection.df$InfctRsk, freq = FALSE, # freq = FALSE for density scale on y-axis
     main = "", # turn off the title as using the fig.cap
     xlab = "Index Value",
     ylab = "Density")
lines(density(infection.df$InfctRsk), col = "blue", lwd = 2)
```
